deep.reconstruction:
This page is a draft of the closing part of the boundary-value discussion in Riemann's 1851 Inauguraldissertation, 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'. In the printed text this material sits in the passage before the conformal-mapping theorem. The page contains no computation; it is a qualitative survey of the kinds of conditions that determine an analytic function w = u + iv of z on a Riemann surface T.

(1) Linked boundary arcs. Two arcs of the boundary of T may be related point by point, P on the first arc corresponding to P' on the second. At each such pair two real equations may hold between the values (u,v) at P and (u,v) at P'. These two real equations can be written as one complex equation F(w(P), w(P')) = 0.

(2) Interior discontinuity lines. Suppose continuity is given up along an interior line L. This case falls under (1): regard L as a boundary arc of each of the two regions it separates, so that its two banks become two related boundary arcs. (The 'jump' conditions across the cuts in the preceding §, where Z changes by a constant, are of this type.)

(3) Extra conditions. Besides these conditions, which hold continuously along whole lines ('equations between arbitrary functions'), further isolated conditions may be needed to fix the function completely. Alternatively, the system of line conditions may itself have to satisfy finitely many side conditions. Riemann says a general survey cannot determine how many.

(4) Geometric interpretation. A completely determined function w(z) maps T, spread over the plane A, onto a surface S covering the plane B. The map is similar in the smallest parts, i.e. conformal where w'(z) ≠ 0.
- The boundary conditions become prescriptions on where the boundary of S lies.
- Case (a), a condition at each boundary point: a family of curves is given, one for each boundary point P of T, and w(P) must lie on its curve. This is the geometric locus of the image of P.
- Case (b), linked arcs: a correspondence between the images of two boundary arcs, so that the image of a point on one arc fixes the image of the related point on the other.

(5) Applications. Applications to particular classes of functions are left outside the scope of the work.
- The case that follows directly from 'our theorem' (the Dirichlet-principle existence theorem of the preceding §§): the loci are a family of parallel straight lines. Prescribing u = Re w on the boundary puts each boundary image on the vertical line Re w = u(P). [My gloss: this is the Dirichlet problem for u, with v determined by the Cauchy-Riemann equations up to a constant.]
- As an illustration Riemann announces the case where all boundary points have the same locus, i.e. the boundary of S is completely given. The next page treats this: the conformal mapping of a simply connected surface onto the unit disc, using log(z − z0) and the Dirichlet integral.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. Two statements are asserted without proof, and Riemann flags them as general remarks: that additional isolated conditions may be needed, and that two real relations can always be packaged as one complex relation. The latter is only formal: the resulting relation need not be holomorphic in w(P), w(P').

results.what: Classification of boundary/transmission conditions for analytic functions: a pointwise relation between u and v on the boundary, a coupling of two boundary arcs (two real equations = one complex equation), and interior discontinuity lines treated as double boundary arcs
results.modern_name: General boundary-value and transmission (Riemann–Hilbert-type / conjugation) problems for analytic functions
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1851 dissertation (statement); systematic theory by Hilbert 1904, Plemelj 1908, Muskhelishvili, Vekua

results.what: Geometric reading: an analytic function maps T conformally onto a surface S over the w-plane; boundary conditions become prescribed loci for the images of boundary points; the Dirichlet case gives parallel straight lines
results.modern_name: Conformal-mapping interpretation of boundary value problems

results.what: Announcement of the case where the whole boundary of the image is given (leading to the Riemann mapping theorem on the next page)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1851 (rigorous proofs by Osgood 1900, Koebe, Carathéodory)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of a passage from Riemann's published 1851 dissertation, closely matching the printed text. Its content is well known and already attributed to him.

transcription_corrections: Line 5: 'complexen[?]' is plausible from the image ('einzigen ...gen' is hard to read). Context requires 'einer einzigen complexen Gleichung', which matches the printed dissertation.
'Abriß' is crossed out before 'allgemeinen Überblick'; 'selbstredend' is uncertain and could also be read as another adverb, but the sense is 'cannot (of course) be determined'.
'von z' should be read as 'Function von z' (complex variable z), as transcribed; the surface S covers plane B.
